slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter nineteen: the examination of time.

slides.heading: Is there time apart from things?
points: Yesterday behind us, tomorrow ahead
We picture time as a river
Would it flow if nothing happened?
slides.say: We live inside time without thinking about it. Yesterday is behind us, tomorrow ahead, and now is the thin edge between them, sliding forward. We picture time as a river that would go on flowing even if nothing happened in it. This chapter, only six verses long, asks whether past, present and future can be found as things in their own right, and whether there is any time at all apart from the things that change.

slides.heading: The shape of the chapter
points: Six verses
What is defined by another cannot stand alone
Continues chapters 2 and 7
slides.say: The reasoning is the same tool used throughout the work: what is defined only in relation to something else cannot also stand on its own. It continues the analysis of motion in chapter two, where the present moment of going could not be found between the gone and the not yet gone, and of arising and ceasing in chapter seven.

slides.heading: The verses
points: A new translation from the Sanskrit
The Sanskrit is shown above each verse
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: Three times that define each other
points: The present: after the past, before the future
'Present' and 'future' are defined by 'past'
How could that relation hold between things?
slides.say: Now the explanation. What makes the present the present? Only that it comes after the past and before the future. Present and future are defined by their relation to past. Verses nineteen point one to three take this ordinary fact seriously, and ask how the relation could hold if each time were a thing in its own right.

slides.heading: Three options, all failing
slides.say: First option. Suppose present and future really depend on the past, as a child depends on a parent who is there. Then they would have to be present in the past, available to be related to. But a present that is already in the past is past, not present. Second option. Suppose instead they are not in the past at all. Then the past has nothing to do with them. How could they depend on something they never meet? Third option. Suppose they do not depend on the past at all. Then they lose what made them present and future. A now with no before is not a now; a later with nothing earlier is not later. So, taken as self-standing items, neither a present nor a future time is found. A relation needs its terms. If each time had its own nature, it would have to meet the others to be related, and meeting would collapse them. The three times hold only as designations made together.

slides.heading: Every pair defined by the other
points: 19.4: start from any time; the same result
High, low, middle; one and many; long and short
Aimed at the Sarvastivada's three real times
slides.say: Verse nineteen point four says the same test works from each starting point. Begin with the future, and the past and present fail in the same way; begin with the present, and so on. It also works for every set of terms defined against each other: high, low and middle; one and many; long and short. Each member is what it is only through the others, so none can be found standing alone. The target here was real. The Sarvastivada school held that the basic elements of experience exist in all three times, past, present and future, and that only their activity changes. Time was given a structure of its own. Nagarjuna's verses take that structure apart.

slides.heading: Can time be caught?
slides.say: Verse nineteen point five approaches from another side. If time were a thing, we could grasp it, pick it out and point to it. Could we? A time that does not stay, that is gone the instant it arrives, cannot be grasped: before we can point to it, it has passed. A time that does stay is not time; a moment that lasts unchanged is not passing, and passing is what time was supposed to be. Only a staying time could be grasped, and a staying time is not time. What we call time is not an item we catch. It is designated on change.

slides.heading: No time apart from things
slides.say: The last verse, nineteen point six, gives the conclusion in two steps. First, if time depends on things, it is not found without things. We know time only through change: the hour by the clock's hands, the year by the seasons, a life by its ageing. Take away every change, and there is nothing left to call time passing. Second, no thing at all is found. This does not mean that nothing appears. It means that no thing is found existing from its own side. So time cannot borrow solidity from things. On the left of the picture is the container: a time that would go on flowing in an empty universe. On the right, before, now and after are designated together with what changes. Neither side is found first.

slides.heading: A lived test: going under
points: Count back from ten; reach seven
A nurse says your name in another room
Three hours on the clock, none in experience
slides.say: The owner's main book gives a lived test. Under a general anaesthetic you count backward from ten, reach seven, and then a nurse is saying your name in another room. Three hours have passed on the clock, and none in experience. If time were a river flowing by itself, it should have carried you through those hours, however unconsciously. It did not. The hours are present in the framework of the operating theatre, recorded and charted, and absent from the framework of your experience. Both are correct within their frame. Neither finds a time that passed on its own.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: Clocks still work; the train still leaves at nine
Time is real as the measure of change
Not a container or river on its own
slides.say: None of this stops clocks from working or appointments from being kept. The train leaves at nine is true, and you can miss it. Physics measures time with great precision, and history orders events reliably. What the chapter removes is the further picture of time as a container or a river that exists before and apart from anything happening. Time is fully real as the measure of change, within the frameworks that measure it. It is simply not a thing on its own. Seeing this has practical weight. The past that seems to press on us and the future that seems to loom are not places where things are stored, waiting. They are designated now, on what appears now.

slides.heading: In the books
points: Substrateless World: the Interlude; Chapters 1 and 8
The Logic of Dependency; Death and Continuity
Talk: Core Logic 3
slides.say: The two books take up these themes in several places. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World: the Interlude, on time; chapter one, where no one has ever met time apart from change; and chapter eight, on going under anaesthesia. The bonus article The Logic of Dependency describes time pictured as a river and as a stuff we spend, and the article Death and Continuity says that under anaesthesia no river of time flowed by itself. There is also a talk on YouTube, Core Logic 3, on the three-way analysis these verses use. Links to all of them are on the chapter page. Next: chapter twenty, the examination of combination.
